evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with jaundice in India: sorting obstructive, parenchymal, infective and isolated (unconjugated) causes from bedside tests, recognising liver failure early, and first treatment before referral. Built on the ICMR Jaundice workflow (July 2020), with NCDC-ICMR antibiotic regimens (2025) for suspected cholangitis.
findings: Bilirubin threshold, four-category classification, symptoms, essential tests (liver function tests (LFT), aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (SGOT, SGPT), alkaline phosphatase) and their patterns, causes, international normalised ratio (INR) warning, referral triggers and management by category (including folic acid 5 mg for haemolysis) checked against the ICMR Jaundice STW (July 2020).
Cholangitis antibiotic regimens with and without sepsis from NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.4; thiamine dose from the ICMR Alcohol Use Disorders STW.
unverifiedSections: Viral hepatitis serology panel (hepatitis A, B, C and E markers) is named in other India topics, not listed in the Jaundice STW; included as standard practice.
Vitamin K, lactulose and antiemetic doses were not given in the opened sources.
Normal laboratory ranges are typical adult values; local ranges apply.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Jaundice is yellow discolouration from raised serum bilirubin; the ICMR workflow uses a threshold above 1.5 mg/dL. Bilirubin rises when too much is made (haemolysis), when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it (hepatitis from viruses, alcohol, drugs such as anti-tubercular therapy, or autoimmunity), or when bile flow is blocked (stones, strictures, cancers of the gallbladder, pancreas or bile ducts). In India, systemic infections such as malaria, enteric fever, dengue, scrub typhus and leptospirosis are common causes with fever. Liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and an ultrasound sort most patients; a rising INR is an early sign of liver failure.
keyMechanisms: Haemolysis overloads conjugation: unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises with normal liver enzymes.
Hepatocyte injury impairs uptake, conjugation and excretion: transaminases rise sharply.
Bile duct obstruction backs up conjugated bilirubin: alkaline phosphatase rises, stools pale, urine darkens, itching.
Loss of synthetic function raises INR and signals liver failure.

symptoms: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, viral prodrome (ICMR STW)
Clay-coloured stools and high-coloured urine (ICMR STW)
redFlags: INR above 1.5 or rising: early liver failure (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Hepatotoxic drugs including anti-tubercular therapy (ICMR STW)
Hepatitis A or E outbreaks (contaminated water)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Alkaline phosphatase over 4–5 times upper limit; dilated bile ducts on ultrasound (ICMR STW).
Transaminases usually over 5 times upper limit (under 500 in alcoholic hepatitis); no duct dilatation (ICMR STW).

differentials.condition: Systemic infection (malaria, enteric fever, dengue, scrub typhus, leptospirosis)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever; positive smear, culture or serology (ICMR STW).
Indirect more than direct bilirubin; normal enzymes and ultrasound (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Alkaline phosphatase over 4–5 times upper limit; normal or mildly raised transaminases; dilated ducts on imaging.
Transaminases usually over 5 times upper limit (under 500 U/L in alcoholic hepatitis); no duct dilatation.
Altered sensorium, bleeding, recurrent vomiting with dehydration, systolic BP below 90 mmHg, or INR above 1.5 or rising.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and classify
actions: Confirm bilirubin above 1.5 mg/dL; do LFT, SGOT, SGPT, alkaline phosphatase and ultrasound (ICMR STW).
Check INR; refer if INR above 1.5 or rising (ICMR STW).
Ask about alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs (including anti-tubercular therapy), fever and travel.

clinicalManagement.title: Obstructive jaundice
actions: IV antibiotics if fever or raised white count (suspected cholangitis) (ICMR STW).

Refer to a centre with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP); definitive treatment by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) or surgery (ICMR STW).
Biliary drainage or relief of obstruction is of utmost importance in sepsis (NTG 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Parenchymal (hepatitis)
actions: Maintain hydration; treat symptoms such as vomiting; normal diet (ICMR STW).
Stop alcohol and all non-prescription drugs (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Isolated raised bilirubin or systemic infection
actions: Haemolysis: folic acid and haematology referral (ICMR STW).
Congenital hyperbilirubinaemia: reassure and refer to confirm (ICMR STW).
Systemic infection: treat the specific illness (ICMR STW).

medicationPlan.note: The Jaundice STW names folic acid 5 mg, IV antibiotics for suspected cholangitis and thiamine for alcoholic hepatitis; antibiotic regimens follow NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.4 (acute cholecystitis and cholangitis), and the thiamine dose the ICMR Alcohol Use Disorders STW. Definitive treatment of obstruction is drainage. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Classify jaundice from LFT pattern and ultrasound.
Know when antibiotics and drainage are urgent.
keyPoints: Alkaline phosphatase over 4–5 times upper limit with dilated ducts: obstruction.
Fever with obstruction: antibiotics and drainage.
pitfalls: Missing malaria, leptospirosis or scrub typhus as the cause of fever with jaundice.
Continuing hepatotoxic drugs or herbal products.
Antibiotics alone without draining an obstructed infected system.
